title: "Study B: is bacterial vaginosis more common in one arm?"

  warning: false

**Where we got to — the story so far.** Three documents, in the order we
made them:

| # | Document | Question | Answer in one line |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `01-qc.qmd` | Is the data good enough to analyse? | Yes — all six files agree, no failed samples; three flags to carry forward |
| 2 | `02-community-composition.qmd` | Do the arms differ in community *composition*? | No evidence — arm explains ~3% of distances, p = 0.15 |
| 3 | this one | Is **BV** more common in one arm? | No evidence — rates 49% / 36% / 38%, p = 0.45; explained below |

This one asks the simplest version of the contraception question: one
person, one BV label (from the Nugent score), which arm are they in?

Two definitions of BV are available and we use both, because they answer
slightly different questions:

- **The clinical label**, `bv` in the metadata, derived from the Nugent score
  (Gram-stain microscopy: 0–3 negative, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 positive).
  This is what a clinician would call BV.
- **The molecular community**, from Tuesday's anatomy module: the fraction of
  each sample's reads that belong to *Lactobacillus*, split at 0.5 into
  `lactobacillus` vs `anaerobe` communities.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
set.seed(2026)

d <- read_counts("group_b")   # all six Study B files
meta <- d$metadata
```

## The answer first, in plain words

If you only read one section, read this one; everything after it is the
working that backs it up. It is also computed from the data, so the table
cannot drift away from the truth.

```{r}
#| label: answer-table
answer_table <- meta |>
  count(arm, name = "people") |>
  left_join(
    meta |> filter(bv == "positive") |> count(arm, name = "bv_positive"),
    by = "arm"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    bv_positive = coalesce(bv_positive, 0),
    rate = scales::percent(bv_positive / people, accuracy = 0.1)
  )
knitr::kable(answer_table)   # as a proper table, not console text
```

Injectable looks highest. **But the answer is no: there is no evidence that
BV is more common in one arm.** Three reasons, in order of how much each
matters:

**1. The gap between the arms is smaller than the noise.** With only 26–39
people per arm, the counts bounce around on their own: ask 39 people on the
street and sometimes 19 say yes, sometimes 10, with nothing real behind the
difference. The largest gap here is 13 percentage points (injectable 48.7%
vs pill 35.7%) — exactly the size of gap that luck produces easily. The
prevalence plot in section 1 shows it: every arm's uncertainty bar covers
the other arms' estimates.

**2. The formal test says the same thing.** Fisher's exact test asks: "if
arm and BV had nothing to do with each other, how often would pure chance
hand me a table at least this uneven?" Answer: about **45% of the time**
(p = 0.45). A result that luck produces nearly half the time is not
evidence of anything. For contrast: in `02-community-composition.qmd` the
Nugent score explained 24% of community variation at p = 0.001 — that is
what a real signal looks like. This is not one.

**3. Two completely different measures of "BV" agree.** The clinical label
(Nugent score, from Gram-stain microscopy) and the molecular community type
(Lactobacillus-dominated or not, from the sequencing counts) are measured by
totally different methods — and both give the same answer (p = 0.45 and
p = 0.53). If contraception really shifted BV rates, it is very unlikely
both measures would have missed it.

**What this study did *not* show.** It did not show the arms have the same
BV rate — no study can show that. With 28 people in the smallest arm, only a
difference of roughly 36 percentage points or more (say 75% vs 40%) could
have been reliably detected (section 3 works this out). A real 13-point
difference would have been invisible. So the honest summary is:

> **No evidence of a large difference; a modest real difference is
> undetectable in a study this size.** Anyone claiming "contraception
> doesn't affect BV" from these 93 people is claiming more than the data
> support.

The sections below show the working, in the order you would want to check
it: the counts and their uncertainty (section 1), the tests (section 2),
what the study could have detected (section 3), the molecular second opinion
(sections 4–5), and the ways you can catch me being wrong at the end.

## 1. The clinical label, by arm

```{r}
#| label: counts
# The raw counts: one row per person, bv label from the Nugent score.
tab <- table(meta$arm, meta$bv)
tab
addmargins(tab)   # row and column totals — should sum to 93

# Prevalence of a positive (Nugent >= 7) in each arm:
prev <- meta |>
  count(arm, positive = bv == "positive", name = "n") |>
  filter(positive) |>
  left_join(meta |> count(arm, name = "total"), by = "arm") |>
  mutate(prevalence = n / total)
prev
```

Injectable has the highest point estimate — **19 of 39 (48.7%)**, against
10 of 28 (35.7%) on the pill and 10 of 26 (38.5%) in the ring — but those are
small samples. The next plot puts an uncertainty bar on each.

```{r}
#| label: prevalence-plot
# 95% CI for each prevalence, from prop.test() (base R).
prev_ci <- prev |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    lo = prop.test(n, total)$conf.int[1],
    hi = prop.test(n, total)$conf.int[2]
  ) |>
  ungroup()

overall <- sum(prev_ci$n) / sum(prev_ci$total)

ggplot(prev_ci, aes(arm, prevalence)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, "/", total)), vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.8)) +
  labs(
    title = "BV prevalence by arm, with 95% confidence intervals",
    subtitle = paste0("Dashed line = all arms combined (",
                      round(overall * 100), "%). Labels are positives / people."),
    x = NULL, y = "Share with a positive Nugent score"
  )
```

The three bars overlap heavily. Injectable sits highest, but every interval
covers the other two arms' estimates.

## 2. The tests

**What the Fisher exact test does, plainly:** it takes the 3x3 table of
counts and asks how many ways the same 93 people could have been distributed
across the table's cells if the arm and the BV label had nothing to do with
each other. The p-value is the share of those ways at least as lopsided as
the real one. Unlike the chi-square test, it needs no "at least 5 per cell"
rule, which matters here because only 3 people are `intermediate`.
([Fisher's exact test, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%27s_exact_test).)

```{r}
#| label: tests
# Primary: Fisher exact on the full 3 x 3 table.
fisher.test(tab)

# Chi-square agrees (p-value simulated, since cell counts are small):
chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 20000)

# Collapsing intermediate in with negative ("any BV" vs "none") changes nothing:
fisher.test(table(meta$arm, meta$bv == "positive"))

# Pairwise, since "more common in ONE arm" is a pairwise question:
pairs <- combn(c("injectable", "pill", "ring"), 2)
tibble(
  comparison = paste(pairs[1, ], "vs", pairs[2, ]),
  p_value = apply(pairs, 2, function(p) {
    sub <- meta |> filter(arm %in% p)
    fisher.test(table(sub$arm, sub$bv == "positive"))$p.value
  })
)

# And the Nugent score as a whole (not just the >= 7 cut), by arm:
kruskal.test(nugent ~ arm, data = meta)
```

Every way of asking agrees: **no evidence BV is more common in one arm.**

- Fisher exact on the full table: p = **0.45**
- Collapsed to positive vs not: p = 0.56
- All three pairwise comparisons: p = 0.33, 0.46, 1.00 — none close to 0.05,
  so the multiple-testing question ("should we correct for doing three
  tests?") never even comes into play
- Nugent as a number, not a label (Kruskal–Wallis): p = 0.63

## 3. Could this study have seen a difference?

A "not significant" is only meaningful next to what the study could have
detected. With 28 people in the smallest arm, 80% power at alpha 0.05
requires roughly a 36-percentage-point difference (base R's
`power.prop.test`, below); the largest observed gap is 13 points.

```{r}
#| label: power
# What prevalence would the pill arm need, vs 38.5% overall, for 80% power?
power.prop.test(n = 28, p1 = 0.385, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.8)
```

So the honest statement is: **a real 13-point difference between injectable
and pill would have been invisible here** — this study can rule out large
differences, not small ones.

## 4. The anatomy module's view: the molecular community

Tuesday defined a community type from the species table itself: each sample's
*Lactobacillus* fraction of reads, split at 0.5. Ten species count as
*Lactobacillus* here (`Genus == "Lactobacillus"` in the taxonomy file).

```{r}
#| label: molecular
lac_taxa <- d$taxonomy |> filter(Genus == "Lactobacillus") |> pull(taxon)
lac_frac <- colSums(d$species[lac_taxa, ]) / colSums(d$species)

dat <- meta |>
  mutate(
    lacto_fraction = lac_frac[meta$sample_id],
    community = ifelse(lacto_fraction >= 0.5, "lactobacillus", "anaerobe")
  )

# The anaerobe community is the molecular picture of BV. Its prevalence by arm:
table(dat$community, dat$arm)
fisher.test(table(dat$community, dat$arm))

kruskal.test(lacto_fraction ~ arm, data = dat)
```

Same answer from the molecular side: anaerobe communities in 51% / 39% / 54%
of injectable / pill / ring (Fisher p = 0.53); the full *Lactobacillus*
fraction differs no more (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.77).

```{r}
#| label: agreement
# Do the two definitions of BV actually agree? (They should, or we are
# not measuring the same thing twice.)
table(dat$community, dat$bv)
fisher.test(table(dat$community, dat$bv))
```

They agree strongly: 37 of 39 clinically-BV samples are anaerobe communities,
45 of 51 negatives are lactobacillus communities (p < 0.001). The
minority who disagree: 2 clinically-positive samples read as
lactobacillus-dominated, and 6 negatives read as anaerobe-dominated —
worth knowing they exist, and far too few to affect anything above.

## Verdict

**No evidence that BV is more common in one contraceptive arm.** The point
estimates order themselves injectable (49%) > ring (38%) > pill (36%), but
the confidence intervals overlap on every pair, Fisher's exact test gives
p = 0.45, and the molecular community view agrees (p = 0.53). Given the study
sizes, only a difference of about 35 percentage points or more could have
been detected — the observed 13-point gap between the highest and lowest arms
was never going to reach significance.

## How you could catch me being wrong

- **Check the counts by hand.** The `addmargins(tab)` output should have 93
  people total: 39 injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring. If the totals are not 93 I
  have lost or double-counted someone.
- **Recompute one prevalence.** From the printed table: injectable has 19
  positives out of 39. 19/39 = 0.487 — the plot's label says `19/39` and the
  point should sit at 48.7%. If the point is elsewhere, the plot and the
  table disagree.
- **Change `bv == "positive"` to `bv != "negative"`** in the collapsed test.
  It moves the 3 `intermediate` people into the "BV" side. I claim it changes
  nothing (p stays around 0.56 — if it drops below 0.05 I was wrong to
  collapse them).

## Choices made

- Used the clinical `bv` label (Nugent-based) as the primary outcome — alternative not chosen: the molecular community type, which I kept as a secondary view because it is defined from the species table and so is one step further from "what a clinician calls BV".
- Fisher exact test as the primary test — alternative not chosen: chi-square alone, whose "5 per cell" rule of thumb is violated by the 3-person intermediate column (I ran it anyway as a check and it agrees).
- Kept the three-level label (negative / intermediate / positive) in the primary test — alternative not chosen: collapsing to two levels first; I collapsed only as a sensitivity check.
- Reported pairwise comparisons alongside the omnibus test — alternative not chosen: the omnibus alone, since "more common in ONE arm" is by definition a pairwise question.
- No multiple-testing correction across the three pairwise tests — alternative not chosen: Holm correction; irrelevant here because all three p-values (0.33, 0.46, 1.00) are far from any threshold.
- Kept `intermediate` (Nugent 4–6) out of "positive" in the primary contrast — alternative not chosen: counting them as BV-positive, which would use a cut-off the field disagrees on.
- Wilson intervals from `prop.test()` for the prevalence plot — alternative not chosen: the Wald normal interval, which behaves badly at these small counts.
- `power.prop.test` at the smallest arm's n (28) to state what the study could detect — alternative not chosen: reporting only the p-value, which would let "no difference" masquerade as "no detectable difference".
- Community cut-off at 0.5 for the Lactobacillus fraction, as in Tuesday's module — alternative not chosen: 0.3 or 0.8, which Tuesday showed moves a few samples between groups but would not change a prevalence this far from half.
- Dropped no samples — the QC report's flags (shallow `B006`, missing cytokines `B018`/`B029`) do not apply here, because the `bv` label and the lacto fractions of those three samples are all present and unremarkable. Alternative not chosen: excluding them anyway, which would have removed evidence for no reason.
